item.title: Best Gamified Productivity Apps in 2026 (Ranked & Reviewed)
item.description: A comprehensive ranking the top gamified productivity apps available in 2026, covering Dovilo, Habitica, BeeDone, Forest, MainQuest, and others. Highlights each app's reward mechanics, focus-timer depth, platform availability, and pricing.

If you've ever opened a plain to-do list, stared at it for three seconds, and closed it again — you're not alone. Gamified productivity apps solve that exact problem by wrapping real work inside reward loops, visual progress, and the same psychological hooks that make games so hard to put down. In 2026, the category has matured well past novelty, and the best options now span everything from RPG-style habit trackers to AI-agent-connected task systems that build virtual cities as you work.

This guide ranks and reviews the top gamified productivity apps available right now, covering what each one does well, where it falls short, and who it's actually built for.

What Makes a Gamified Productivity App Worth Using?

Not every app that slaps a badge on a completed task deserves to be called gamified. The best ones share a few qualities:

  • A meaningful reward loop. Completing work should produce something you actually want — coins, progress, visual change, or character growth.
  • Depth beyond the first week. Novelty fades fast. Good gamification has enough layers to stay interesting over months.
  • Genuine task management underneath. The game mechanics should sit on top of a functional to-do or focus system, not replace it.
  • A reason to come back daily. Streaks, unlockables, and persistent worlds all help.

With those criteria in mind, here's how the leading apps stack up.

1. Dovilo — Best Overall for 2026

Best for: Productivity seekers who want a persistent visual world, and developers who use AI coding agents daily.

Platforms: iOS, Android, Windows, macOS

Pricing: Free tier available; Pro plans start at $2.49/month

Dovilo is the most distinctive entry in this category in 2026. It combines a smart task manager, a Pomodoro-style focus timer, and an isometric city builder into one cohesive app. Every task you complete and every focus session you finish earns brick, which you spend on buildings and decorations in a virtual city that grows alongside your actual work output.

The city-builder metaphor is what separates Dovilo from the crowd. You're not collecting loot for an RPG character or watching a plant grow — you're constructing a skyline that reflects months of real work. It's calm, design-forward, and satisfying in a way that retro pixel RPGs aren't for everyone.

What makes Dovilo stand out

The free tier is genuinely useful. You get full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, basic city building, dark and light themes, and no ads. That's a strong foundation before you spend anything.

The Pro tier adds something no other gamified productivity app currently offers: a built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) server on the desktop app. This lets AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI, and others execute tasks step-by-step inside Dovilo while you monitor progress from your phone. You set a per-project scope and brief so agents only see what you explicitly allow. Your mobile view shows agent notes, token usage, and cost per task in real time.

For developers who already run AI agents daily, this is a fundamentally different value proposition than anything Habitica or BeeDone offers. Your task list becomes the control surface for your AI workflow, not just a reminder system.

Pro also includes cloud sync across devices, all buildings and decorations, advanced statistics, custom themes, and priority support. The yearly plan saves 33% over monthly, and there's a lifetime option for users who prefer a one-time payment.

Where Dovilo could improve

The app is relatively new, so the city-builder content library will grow over time. Users who want deep social features or party-based accountability (Habitica's strength) won't find that here yet.

Verdict: The most complete gamified productivity app in 2026 for users who want a beautiful persistent world and, for developers, a task system that connects directly to their AI toolchain.

2. Habitica — Best for Deep RPG Gamification

Best for: Users who want the deepest gamification system and community accountability.

Platforms: iOS, Android, Web

Pricing: Free; optional subscription from $4.99/month or $47.99/year

Habitica has been in this category longer than almost anyone, and it shows. Your tasks, habits, and dailies all feed into an RPG character that gains levels, collects gear, and joins parties with other users. The social layer is genuinely strong — guilds, party quests, and accountability groups give Habitica a community feel that most competitors haven't matched.

The gamification is deep. There are pets, mounts, seasonal events, and enough progression layers to stay interesting for years. For ADHD users who need external motivation structures, Habitica's system is well-documented and widely recommended.

The tradeoffs are real, though. The visual style is retro pixel art, which won't appeal to everyone. The focus timer isn't a core feature. There's no persistent world you're building — the reward is character progression and loot, not a growing environment. And there's no MCP or agent-execution layer for developers.

Verdict: The strongest choice if community accountability and deep RPG mechanics are your priority. Less suitable if you want modern aesthetics, a focus-first workflow, or AI agent integration.

3. BeeDone — Best for AI Coaching on Mobile

Best for: Mobile-first users who want AI-powered motivation alongside gamified tasks.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free to start; in-app purchases (specific pricing not clearly public)

BeeDone takes a modern approach to gamified productivity, combining task management, XP systems, deep-work timers, and AI coaching in a mobile-first package. It's explicitly designed for procrastination and decision paralysis, and the AI coaching layer adds a dimension that pure gamification apps lack.

The app targets ADHD and neurodivergent users well, with features designed to reduce friction at the moment you're most likely to avoid starting. The visual design is cleaner than Habitica's.

Where BeeDone falls short is in the depth of its world. The reward system feels like an overlay on a to-do app rather than a persistent environment you're genuinely building. Pricing transparency is also weaker than it should be — it's hard to know what you're paying before you're inside the app. There's no city-builder metaphor and no MCP integration for developers.

Verdict: A solid option for mobile-focused users who want AI coaching woven into their gamified workflow. Less compelling for those who want a distinctive visual world or desktop agent connectivity.

4. Forest — Best Single-Focus Timer App

Best for: Users who want a simple, proven focus mechanic with real-world impact.

Platforms: iOS, Android, Chrome extension

Pricing: Free with in-app purchases

Forest is one of the most recognized apps in the focus-timer space, and for good reason. You plant a virtual tree when you start a focus session; if you leave the app, the tree dies. Finish the session and your forest grows. The app also partners with Trees for the Future to plant real trees, which adds genuine meaning to the mechanic.

The simplicity is both Forest's strength and its ceiling. It does one thing extremely well and doesn't try to do much else. There's no full task management system, no persistent world beyond your growing forest, and no AI layer. If you want a focus timer with light gamification and a clear conscience about your screen time, Forest is excellent. If you want a complete productivity system with deeper rewards, you'll outgrow it.

Verdict: The best standalone focus timer with gamification. Not a full productivity system, but a benchmark for how simple mechanics can create genuine daily habits.

5. MainQuest — Best for Quest-Framed Task Management

Best for: Users who strongly dislike traditional to-do lists and respond better to game framing.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free to start; specific pricing not public

MainQuest reframes your entire task list as a quest log. Tasks become missions, you earn XP, your character grows, and the whole experience is designed to make productivity feel less like a chore. The messaging is clear and the anti-checklist positioning resonates with users who've bounced off every standard productivity app.

The app is more character-centric than world-building-centric, which makes it feel closer to Habitica than to Dovilo. There's less evidence of deep focus-timer functionality or an AI integration layer. Pricing opacity is a real friction point for anyone trying to evaluate value before committing.

Verdict: A good fit for users who need game framing to engage with their tasks at all. Less suitable for users who want a full ecosystem or developer workflow integration.

6. Focus Plant — Best for Collectible Focus Rewards

Best for: Users who want a focus timer tied to a growing virtual garden with collectible elements.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free with in-app purchases

Focus Plant sits closer to Dovilo's reward loop than Forest does, because it converts focus time into resources that grow a virtual environment. You collect plants, manage a garden, and the app includes distraction-blocking features to keep you on task.

The scope is narrower than it looks, though. Focus Plant is primarily a focus timer and plant collection game rather than a full task management system. There's no integrated to-do layer, no desktop app, and no AI connectivity. If you want a visually satisfying focus reward that goes slightly deeper than Forest, Focus Plant delivers. If you want task orchestration alongside the rewards, you'll need something else.

Verdict: A pleasant middle ground between Forest's simplicity and a full gamified productivity suite. Best as a focus companion rather than a primary task system.

7. LifeAt — Best for Ambient Workspace Aesthetics

Best for: Users who want a beautiful digital workspace environment with light planning tools.

Platforms: Web

Pricing: Free tier; Pro at $8/month billed yearly or $12/month billed monthly

LifeAt creates ambient virtual spaces — think cozy rooms, cafes, or nature scenes — that you work inside. It includes a planner, calendar, and focus timer, all wrapped in a visually appealing environment. The mood it creates is genuinely pleasant.

The distinction worth making: LifeAt is about workspace aesthetics rather than a reward economy. You're not earning anything or building anything based on your output. The environment is static and decorative rather than dynamic and responsive to your work. That makes it more of a focus environment than a gamified productivity app in the traditional sense.

Verdict: Strong for users who want their workspace to feel nicer. Not the right choice if you want your environment to respond to and reward your actual output.

8. Amazing Marvin — Best for Customizable Workflow Depth

Best for: Productivity enthusiasts and ADHD users who need extreme workflow flexibility.

Platforms: Web, iOS, Android, Desktop

Pricing: $8/month billed yearly ($96/year)

Amazing Marvin is one of the most customizable task managers available. It supports dozens of anti-procrastination strategies, flexible scheduling systems, and deep workflow configuration that most apps don't come close to matching. For users who've tried every productivity system and found them all too rigid, Marvin is often the answer.

The gamification angle is thin, though. There are some reward elements, but the experience is fundamentally functional rather than playful. There's no persistent visual world, no meaningful game loop, and the interface prioritizes power over delight. If you're here because you want gamification, Marvin probably isn't your app.

Verdict: Exceptional for workflow depth and customization. Not a gamified productivity app in any meaningful sense — it's a serious planning tool.

9. Finch — Best for Gentle, Emotional Gamification

Best for: Users who want a low-pressure, wellness-oriented progression system.

Platforms: iOS, Android

Pricing: Free with in-app purchases

Finch is a self-care pet app where a small bird grows as you complete habits and check-ins. The emotional tone is deliberately gentle and guilt-free, which makes it approachable for users who find harder gamification systems stressful. It has strong mainstream appeal and genuinely positive user sentiment.

The tradeoff is scope. Finch is oriented toward mental wellness and self-care rather than task execution or work productivity. There's no focus timer depth, no desktop app, and no developer workflow integration. It proves that emotionally resonant gamification works — but it's solving a different problem than most users searching for productivity apps need solved.

Verdict: Excellent for its intended use case of gentle habit-building and self-care. Not the right tool if you need a serious work productivity system.

How the Apps Compare at a Glance

App Task Management Focus Timer Visual World AI/MCP Free Tier
Dovilo Full Pomodoro City builder Yes (Pro) Yes
Habitica Full Basic RPG character No Yes
BeeDone Full Deep work Overlays AI coaching Yes
Forest None Core feature Forest No Yes
MainQuest Full Limited Character No Yes
Focus Plant None Core feature Garden No Yes
LifeAt Light Basic Static spaces No Yes
Amazing Marvin Full Basic None No No
Finch Habits only None Pet No Yes

Which Gamified Productivity App Should You Choose?

The right app depends on what's actually blocking you.

If you want the most complete combination of task management, focus sessions, visual world-building, and AI agent integration in one app, Dovilo is the standout choice in 2026. It's the only app that connects your task list directly to AI coding agents while also giving you a persistent city that grows from your real work output.

If community accountability and deep RPG mechanics matter most, Habitica is the proven option. If you just need a clean focus timer with a satisfying mechanic, Forest still delivers. And if you're an ADHD user who wants AI coaching on mobile, BeeDone is worth trying.

Most of these apps have free tiers, so the practical advice is to try the one that fits your primary use case and see whether the reward loop keeps you coming back after the first week. That's the real test of any gamification system.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a gamified productivity app? A gamified productivity app uses game mechanics — points, rewards, visual progression, unlockables, or narrative framing — to make completing tasks and maintaining focus more motivating. The goal is to create an intrinsic reward loop that keeps you returning to your work system consistently.

Is Dovilo free to use? Yes. Dovilo has a free tier that includes full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, basic city building, dark and light themes, and no ads. Pro plans add cloud sync, the desktop app, MCP/AI agent integration, all buildings and decorations, advanced statistics, and custom themes.

What is the best Habitica alternative in 2026? Dovilo is the strongest Habitica alternative for users who want a modern visual world rather than a retro RPG aesthetic, or for developers who want their task list connected to AI agents. BeeDone is a good alternative for mobile-first users who want AI coaching. MainQuest works well for users who want quest framing over RPG mechanics.

What does MCP mean in a productivity app? MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI agents communicate with external tools and services. In Dovilo's case, the built-in MCP server on the desktop app allows AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI to read and execute tasks step-by-step, with the user monitoring progress from their phone.

Can gamified productivity apps help with ADHD? Many users with ADHD report that gamified apps help significantly with task initiation and follow-through, because the reward loop provides immediate feedback that plain to-do lists don't. Habitica, BeeDone, and Dovilo are all commonly recommended in ADHD productivity communities for different reasons.

Is Forest still worth using in 2026? Forest remains excellent as a standalone focus timer with a satisfying mechanic and a real-world impact through tree planting. It's not a full task management system, so users who need more than a focus timer will likely want to pair it with another app or switch to something like Dovilo that includes both.

Which gamified productivity app is best for developers? Dovilo is the only app in this category with a built-in MCP server that connects AI coding agents directly to your task list. If you use Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or similar tools daily, Dovilo's Pro tier gives you task oversight and agent execution in one place — something no other gamified productivity app currently offers.

The gamified productivity space in 2026 has real options at every level of complexity. Start with the app that matches where you are right now, not where you think you should be. A city that grows from your actual work is more motivating than a perfect system you never open.

item.title: Todoist Alternative: 7 Apps Worth Switching To in 2026
item.description: Find the best Todoist alternative in 2026 — from gamified apps to AI-native tools — with honest notes on who each one suits best.
item.content:encoded:
On this page

  • What Makes a Good Todoist Alternative?
  • 7 Todoist Alternatives Worth Switching To in 2026
    • 1. Dovilo
    • 2. Habitica
    • 3. TickTick
    • 4. Amazing Marvin
    • 5. Forest
    • 6. Sunsama
    • 7. BeeDone
  • How to Choose Between These Apps
  • A Closer Look at Dovilo for Developers
  • Quick Comparison
  • Frequently Asked Questions
  • The Bottom Line

Todoist is a genuinely solid task manager. Clean interface, reliable sync, good keyboard shortcuts. But if you've been using it for a while and something still feels off — no motivation, no focus support, no real reason to open the app — you're not alone. Most people searching for a Todoist alternative in 2026 want one of three things: more gamification, better focus tools, or something that actually connects to their AI coding workflow.

This list covers seven apps worth a real look, with honest notes on who each one suits best.

What Makes a Good Todoist Alternative?

It depends entirely on why you're leaving.

Todoist's strengths are natural language input, project hierarchy, and cross-platform reliability. Its weakness, for a lot of users, is motivational: there's no intrinsic reward for finishing tasks beyond the satisfaction of checking a box. If you're a student, a developer, or anyone who needs external feedback loops to stay consistent, that gap matters more than it sounds.

A strong alternative should cover the basics — due dates, priorities, recurring tasks — and add something Todoist doesn't. Every app below brings a distinct angle.

7 Todoist Alternatives Worth Switching To in 2026

1. Dovilo

Best for: Gamified productivity seekers and AI-native developers who want task management, focus timers, and a visual reward system in one place.

Dovilo takes a different approach to the whole idea of a to-do list. The core loop is simple: complete tasks and focus sessions, earn bricks, spend bricks to grow an isometric city. Every item you finish translates into something visible — a new building, a park, a landmark added to your virtual city.

The task layer covers everything you'd expect: due dates, priorities, categories, and recurring tasks. The Pomodoro-style focus timer awards bricks per session, so focused work and task completion both feed the same reward system. On mobile, it runs on iOS and Android. On desktop (Windows and macOS), the Pro plan adds a built-in MCP server.

That MCP server is what makes Dovilo genuinely different for developers. It lets AI coding agents — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cursor CLI, Windsurf, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI — pick up tasks from your list, execute them step by step, and report back. Each project can be scoped with a brief so agents only see what you've explicitly permitted. A mobile telemetry view shows agent notes, token usage, and cost per task, so you can monitor what's running without being at your desk.

Storage is offline-first, so the app works without a network connection. Cloud sync is a Pro feature.

Pricing: The free tier includes full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, and basic city building with no ads. Pro Yearly is $19.99 per year ($1.67 per month), Pro Monthly is $2.49 per month, and Pro Lifetime is a one-time $49.99 payment. A 7-day free Pro trial is available with no charge if cancelled before it ends.

Where it falls short: The city builder is a reward and visualization layer, not a standalone game. If you want deep RPG mechanics or a large social community, Habitica has more of that. The MCP and AI agent features are Pro and desktop-only.

2. Habitica

Best for: People who want RPG-style gamification with an established community.

Habitica turns your task list into a role-playing game. You build a character, earn gear, join parties with other users, and fight monsters by completing habits and dailies. The community is large and active, and the accountability mechanics — where your party members take damage if you miss a daily — are genuinely effective for some people.

The visual style is retro pixel art, which either feels charming or dated depending on your taste. There's no meaningful focus timer, and no MCP or agent-execution layer. If you're a developer looking for workflow integration, Habitica won't help there.

Where it fits: Students or anyone who responds well to social accountability and RPG progression.

3. TickTick

Best for: Users who want a Todoist-like experience with a built-in Pomodoro timer.

TickTick is probably the closest direct replacement for Todoist on this list. Natural language input, project folders, tags, priority levels, calendar view — it's all there. The built-in Pomodoro timer is a meaningful addition that Todoist doesn't offer natively.

The free tier is more limited than Todoist's, and the Premium plan runs around $35.99 per year. The interface is clean and the mobile apps are well-made. There's no gamification layer and no AI agent integration.

Where it fits: Power users who want Todoist's feature set plus a focus timer, without significantly changing their workflow.

4. Amazing Marvin

Best for: People with ADHD or complex productivity systems who want deep customization.

Amazing Marvin is built around the idea that no single productivity system works for everyone. You can configure it to behave like GTD, time-blocking, the Ivy Lee method, or a hybrid of all three. The customization depth is genuinely impressive — gamification elements exist, but as optional modules rather than a core identity.

There's no visual reward system and no focus timer built in by default. It's a tool for people who want to engineer their own system rather than adopt someone else's.

Where it fits: Productivity enthusiasts, especially those who've tried multiple systems and want something they can shape precisely.

5. Forest

Best for: People who primarily want a focus timer with a visual reward and a real-world mission.

Forest is a focus timer first. You plant a virtual tree when you start a session; it dies if you leave the app. The app also partners with a tree-planting organization, so your focus sessions contribute to real reforestation.

It's not a task manager. No to-do list, no project management, no AI integration. But if your main complaint about Todoist is that it doesn't support focused work sessions, Forest handles that one thing very well.

Where it fits: Anyone who wants a clean, mission-driven focus timer and doesn't need task management in the same app.

6. Sunsama

Best for: Professionals who want a structured daily planning ritual with calendar integration and AI features.

Sunsama sits at the opposite end of the motivation spectrum from gamified apps. It's calm, structured, and intentional. The daily planning ritual pulls tasks from integrations — Asana, Linear, GitHub, and others — and you schedule them into time blocks for the day. The Pro plan includes AI features and MCP support, which is worth noting for developers who want a planning-first workflow.

At $20 per month billed yearly, it's one of the more expensive options here. The audience is professionals who want a thoughtful planning process, not a reward system.

Where it fits: People who want structured daily planning with deep calendar and project tool integration, and who have no interest in gamification.

7. BeeDone

Best for: Mobile-first users who want gamified tasks with AI coaching.

BeeDone combines task management with XP, levels, and AI coaching in a mobile-first interface. It's lighter than Habitica in terms of RPG depth but more approachable. There's no persistent world metaphor — you level up a character rather than build something — and pricing isn't publicly listed.

The AI coaching angle is interesting if you want suggestions on how to approach your tasks, though the depth of that feature varies.

Where it fits: Users who want a mobile-first gamified experience with some AI guidance and don't need desktop or agent integration.

How to Choose Between These Apps

The right pick depends on what's actually missing from your Todoist setup.

If you want motivation through visible rewards: Dovilo and Habitica are the strongest options. Dovilo gives you a city to build toward; Habitica gives you a character to develop and a community to stay accountable with.

If you want a near-direct Todoist replacement with more features: TickTick is the easiest transition. The learning curve is minimal and the feature overlap is high.

If you're a developer using AI coding agents: Dovilo is the only app on this list that connects task management to agent execution via MCP. Scoped project briefs, step-by-step agent execution, and mobile telemetry for token usage and cost — that workflow doesn't exist anywhere else in this category.

If you want calm over motivation: Sunsama is the premium option for structured daily planning. It won't gamify your work, but it will help you plan it deliberately.

If focus sessions are your main gap: Forest handles that single job better than most. Dovilo handles it within a broader system.

A Closer Look at Dovilo for Developers

The MCP angle is worth a closer look because it's genuinely new territory for productivity apps.

When you connect Claude Code, Cursor, or another supported agent to Dovilo's desktop MCP server, the agent can see your task list within the scope you've defined, pick up a task, execute it, and mark it complete. A project brief limits what the agent can access, so your personal tasks stay separate from what you've explicitly permitted it to see.

The mobile telemetry view lets you watch this happen from your phone in real time — agent notes, token usage, and cost per task. If you're running long coding sessions and want to delegate specific subtasks to an agent while you handle others yourself, it's a workflow worth exploring.

Auto-generated JSON config snippets handle the MCP client setup, which cuts down the friction of getting started. The feature is Pro and desktop-only, but at $1.67 per month on the yearly plan — or $49.99 for lifetime access — the barrier to try it is low.

Quick Comparison

App Focus Timer Gamification AI/MCP Integration Free Tier
Dovilo Yes (Pomodoro) City builder Yes (Pro, desktop) Yes, no ads
Habitica No RPG/avatar No Yes
TickTick Yes (Pomodoro) No No Limited
Amazing Marvin Optional Optional modules No Trial only
Forest Yes Visual tree No Limited
Sunsama No No Yes (Pro) No
BeeDone No XP/levels AI coaching Unclear

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best free Todoist alternative? Dovilo's free tier includes full to-do management, unlimited focus sessions, and basic city building with no ads — one of the more generous free options on this list. Habitica also has a free tier with its full RPG system. TickTick's free plan is more limited.

Which Todoist alternative is best for developers? Dovilo is the strongest option for developers who use AI coding agents. Its built-in MCP server (Pro, desktop) connects to Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and other agents, letting them execute tasks from your list with per-project scope controls and mobile telemetry.

Is there a Todoist alternative with a Pomodoro timer built in? Yes. Both Dovilo and TickTick include built-in Pomodoro-style focus timers. Dovilo ties the timer to a coin reward system that feeds the city builder; TickTick's timer is more straightforward.

What's the cheapest Todoist alternative with Pro features? Dovilo Pro Yearly works out to $1.67 per month ($19.99 per year), which is among the lowest price points for a productivity app with cloud sync, focus timer, gamification, and AI agent integration. The Pro Lifetime option at $49.99 is a one-time payment with no recurring charge.

Is Habitica better than Todoist for motivation? For users who respond to social accountability and RPG progression, Habitica's party system and avatar mechanics can be more motivating than Todoist's plain task list. The trade-off is no focus timer and a more complex interface. Dovilo offers a different gamification model — a city builder rather than an RPG — with a simpler entry point.

Can I use a Todoist alternative offline? Dovilo stores data locally by default and works without a network connection. Cloud sync is available on Pro. Most other apps on this list require a connection for sync, though some cache data locally.

Which Todoist alternative is best for ADHD? Amazing Marvin is specifically designed with ADHD users in mind, offering deep customization of task views and workflows. Dovilo's visual reward system and focus timer can also help with motivation and follow-through, which are common challenges for ADHD users. The right choice depends on whether you need customization depth or external motivation mechanics.

The Bottom Line

Todoist does a lot of things well, but "well" isn't always enough if you're not opening the app. The best alternative depends on what's actually causing the friction — lack of motivation, missing focus support, or a workflow that doesn't connect to how you work today.

If you want a to-do list that gives you something to build toward, connects to your AI coding agents, and doesn't cost much to try, Dovilo is worth downloading. The free tier is a solid starting point, and the Pro features — especially the MCP integration for developers — are priced low enough to test properly. It also offers a one-week free trial period.
